articles.title: 500,000-year-old elephant bone hammer shows ancient humans were master toolmakers
articles.summary: Early humans in England crafted a rare piece of elephant bone into a reusable hammer for sharpening stone tools nearly 500,000 years ago. The extraordinary find reveals that ancient toolmakers were resourceful, skilled, and capable of surprisingly advanced planning.
articles.content:
Archaeologists have identified a prehistoric hammer made from elephant bone that dates back almost 500,000 years. Found in southern England, the object is the oldest known elephant bone tool ever discovered in Europe.

Researchers from UCL and the Natural History Museum, London analyzed the rare artifact, which offers a striking look at the intelligence and technical abilities of early human ancestors. Their findings were published in Science Advances.

The tool was probably created by early neanderthals or Homo heidelbergensis. Rather than serving as a heavy hammer, it functioned as a softer striking tool used to repair and sharpen stone handaxes and other cutting implements after their edges became worn.

Lead author Simon Parfitt (UCL Institute of Archaeology and Scientific Associate at the Natural History Museum) said: "This remarkable discovery showcases the ingenuity and resourcefulness of our ancient ancestors. They possessed, not only a deep knowledge of the local materials around them, but also a sophisticated understanding of how to craft highly refined stone tools. Elephant bone would have been a rare but highly useful resource, and it's likely this was a tool of considerable value."

A 500,000-Year-Old Elephant Bone Tool

The fossilized object has a roughly triangular shape. It measures approximately 11 centimeters long, six centimeters in width, and about three centimeters thick. Marks across its surface show that early humans deliberately shaped it for use as a tool.

Most of the fragment consists of cortical bone, the thick and dense tissue that forms the hard outer layer of bones. Its unusual thickness indicates that it came from either an elephant or a mammoth. However, too little of the original bone remains for researchers to identify the exact animal species or determine which part of the skeleton it came from.

The fragment was first recovered during the early 1990s. At the time, researchers did not recognize it as a tool. Its true purpose only became clear after scientists recently carried out a more detailed examination of objects recovered from the site.

Microscopic Clues Reveal Its Purpose

The team studied the bone with 3D scanning technology and electron microscopes. Their analysis revealed distinctive notches, impact damage and other signs that the object had repeatedly been used as a hammer.

Tiny pieces of flint were also found lodged inside the marks. These fragments provided strong evidence that the bone had been used to strike, reshape and maintain stone tools on multiple occasions.

Because bone is softer than stone, it allows a toolmaker to work more precisely without causing excessive damage. Early humans often used bone implements to sharpen the cutting edges of handaxes and tools used for butchering animals.

Researchers concluded that the object probably acted as a "retoucher." A retoucher is used to strike the edge of a worn stone tool, knocking off small flakes to restore its intended form and cutting edge. This method of shaping stone is known as "knapping."

Elephant bone would have been especially suitable for this task. Its dense outer layer was harder and more durable than the bones of many other animals available in the region, allowing it to withstand repeated impacts.

A Rare and Valuable Prehistoric Resource

Elephants and mammoths were not common in prehistoric southern England. The decision to collect, preserve and shape such a rare material provides evidence of the resourcefulness and mental abilities of the early humans living there.

They appear to have understood that elephant bone offered advantages over more widely available animal bones. Instead of treating it as waste, they recognized its value and saved it for a specialized purpose.

The use of a retoucher also points to a relatively advanced level of technology. With this tool, early humans could create and maintain stone implements that were more carefully shaped and complex than those produced by some other prehistoric populations living during the same period.

Co-author Dr. Silvia Bello, Merit Researcher at the Natural History Museum, said: "Our ancient ancestors were sophisticated in their use of tools. Collecting and shaping an elephant bone fragment and then using it on multiple occasions to shape and sharpen stone tools shows an advanced level of complex thinking and abstract thought. They were resourceful gatherers of available materials, and savvy about how best to use them."

The Boxgrove Archaeological Site

The elephant bone tool came from Boxgrove, an archaeological site near Chichester in West Sussex, England. Boxgrove has been extensively excavated, and researchers have uncovered many tools made from flint, bone and antler there.

Until now, however, no tool made from elephant bone had been identified at the site.

Scientists do not know whether early humans hunted the animal or collected its bone from a carcass that was already dead. Damage and deformation on the artifact suggest that the bone was still relatively fresh when it was shaped and used.

An Exceptionally Rare European Discovery

Elephant bone tools have previously been found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, with some examples dating back as far as 1.5 million years.

In Europe, however, discoveries of ancient elephant bone tools are extremely uncommon. Only a small number are known from before 43,000 years ago, when modern humans (Homo sapiens) began spreading across the continent and produced large quantities of ivory and elephant bone tools, artworks and structures.

Before this discovery, no European elephant bone tool was known to be older than approximately 450,000 years. Most of those early examples were also found much farther south, in regions with warmer climates.

The Boxgrove artifact therefore expands the known history and geographical range of elephant bone technology in Europe. It also reveals that early humans in Britain were carefully selecting rare materials and using them to produce and maintain highly refined tools hundreds of thousands of years ago.

The research was supported by English Heritage, UCL and the Calleva Foundation.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant archaeological discovery revealing advanced toolmaking skills of early humans nearly 500,000 years ago. This finding provides meaningful insight into human technological evolution and cognitive abilities, with broad significance for understanding human history and prehistory. The detailed analysis and context demonstrate a substantial breakthrough in knowledge about ancient human technology.

articles.title: Pyridoxal photoenzymes for asymmetric radical–radical cross-couplings
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 27 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10930-9Pyridoxal photoenzymes for asymmetric radical–radical cross-couplings
articles.content: Non-native photoenzymes have enabled a myriad of asymmetric bond-forming events that are otherwise challenging or currently impossible with small molecule catalysis.1,2 These reactions require enzymes with cofactors that are strong absorbers in the visible region with reasonably long-lived excited states, such as flavin and nicotinamide. However, there exists a substantial chromophoric cofactor “dark space” where no known photoenzymatic activity has been characterized.1 Increased knowledge of the photophysics of the cofactors in the “dark space” would increase the types of bonds that photoenzymes can form by accessing new excited state intermediates in enzyme classes with divergent reactivities and selectivities. Here, we establish pyridoxal 5’-phosphate (PLP) as a photoenzymatic cofactor by leveraging the excited state quinonoid intermediate as a potent single-electron reductant. We overcome the poor photophysical properties of the native quinonoid intermediate by employing non-native benzyl amine substrates and exploiting Förster resonance energy transfer mechanism from an exogenous photosensitizer to access the quinonoid excited state. This redox neutral approach enables an asymmetric radical-radical cross-coupling between benzyl amines and reductive radical precursors through concomitant generation and localization of a radical pair in an enzyme active site—overcoming the typical challenges associated with this reaction by removing the necessity for radical sorting and the persistent radical effect. 33 The emergent photoexcited intermediates of PLP identified in this work greatly expands the potential avenues for valuable bond forming events by PLP-dependent enzymes.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in enzymatic catalysis using pyridoxal photoenzymes to enable asymmetric radical-radical cross-couplings, a reaction previously challenging or impossible. This discovery expands the potential for new bond-forming reactions, which can have broad implications in chemical synthesis and pharmaceutical development, benefiting society at large.
articles.personality_title: New enzyme method creates complex chemical bonds using light
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists often use enzymes with special helpers called cofactors to speed up chemical reactions, especially those involving light. Some cofactors work well with visible light, but many types have not been explored for light-driven reactions.

**What happened** – Researchers discovered that pyridoxal 5’-phosphate (PLP), a common enzyme cofactor, can be used as a light-activated helper to create complex chemical bonds. They used a trick involving light energy transfer from another molecule to activate PLP, allowing it to join two radical molecules in a precise way. This method works with benzyl amines and other radical precursors to form new bonds that were difficult to make before.

**Impact** – This discovery opens up new possibilities for making complex molecules more efficiently. Since the method controls how the two radicals join, it can help produce chemicals with specific shapes, which is important for making medicines and other materials. It also uses light in a clever way to activate enzymes that were not known to work with light before.

**What's next step** – Scientists will likely explore how to use this approach with other enzymes and molecules. This could lead to new ways to build important chemicals, making drug development and material science faster and more precise.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists found a new light-powered enzyme method to create complex chemical bonds that were previously hard to form, promising advances in chemistry and medicine.

articles.title: These insect submariners survive depths that should crush them
articles.summary: Lake fly larvae plunge more than 200 meters into Lake Malawi each day to hide from predators, using tiny air sacs to control their depth. A rubber-like material called resilin lets them expand or shrink the sacs by changing their pH. Their toughness challenges a popular explanation for why insects are absent from the open ocean.
articles.content:
Deep-diving insect larvae in an African lake are forcing scientists to reconsider a popular explanation for why insects are almost entirely absent from the open ocean. Their secret is a remarkably durable system of air sacs that can tolerate far more pressure than researchers expected.

Billions of lake fly larvae (Chaoborus edulis), living in Lake Malawi in East Africa, complete an extraordinary vertical migration every day.

During daylight hours, the larvae descend more than 200 meters into a deep region of the lake with very little oxygen. This area, often called a dead zone, offers shelter from predators that cannot easily survive there. After dark, the larvae rise toward the surface to feed, although they must first pass through large numbers of fish waiting to eat them.

To track this daily movement, UBC researchers Drs. Philip Matthews and Evan McKenzie placed a sonar system on the lake floor. The equipment allowed them to observe the enormous groups of larvae as they moved through the water.

Tiny Air Sacs Work Like Ballast Tanks

When the researchers examined the larvae, they discovered that the insects had adapted part of their respiratory system into two pairs of small air sacs.

These sacs act much like the ballast tanks of a submarine. By adjusting their size, the larvae can change their buoyancy and control whether they rise or sink in the lake.

The walls of the sacs contain resilin, an unusually elastic material found in many insects. The larvae can alter the pH of the sac walls, causing the resilin to expand or contract. This changes the volume of the air sacs and gives the larvae precise control over their depth.

Air Sacs Survive Extreme Water Pressure

The researchers next placed the larvae inside miniature pressure chambers to determine how much pressure the air sacs could withstand before collapsing.

The results were striking. The sacs survived pressures equal to those found at depths of more than 400 meters, which is far deeper than the larvae normally travel during their daily migration.

Insects are highly successful on land and in fresh water, yet the open ocean contains virtually none. One widely discussed explanation is that the intense pressure at greater depths would crush the air spaces used by insects for breathing.

The toughness of these larvae suggests that pressure alone may not fully explain why insects never established themselves throughout the ocean.

Biological Rubber Could Inspire New Materials

Scientists have previously studied resilin because it behaves almost like a perfect biological rubber. In other insects, it helps form durable structures such as wing hinges and tendons that must bend repeatedly without wearing out.

The newly discovered buoyancy system could also contribute to efforts to develop smart materials made with resilin. Researchers may eventually use similar mechanisms to create artificial muscles or other materials that move when triggered by a chemical change in pH.

This project was partially funded by Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada Discovery and Accelerator grants.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about insect larvae with a unique biological adaptation that challenges existing explanations about insect absence in the ocean. This finding has broad implications for biology and materials science, potentially inspiring new smart materials with real-world applications.
articles.personality_title: Insect larvae use tiny air sacs to dive deep in Lake Malawi
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Insects are rarely found in the open ocean, and scientists have thought this is because deep water pressure crushes their air-filled body parts. But some insect larvae living in Lake Malawi, Africa, dive very deep every day, challenging this idea.

They use small air sacs in their bodies like submarine tanks to control their depth. These sacs are made with a stretchy material called resilin, which changes size when the larvae adjust the acidity (pH) inside the sacs. Tests showed these sacs can survive pressures found even twice as deep as the larvae usually go.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that pressure alone may not explain why insects don’t live in the ocean’s depths. The larvae’s air sacs are tougher than expected, suggesting other reasons must keep insects from living in the deep ocean. Also, the stretchy resilin material could inspire new inventions, like artificial muscles or smart materials that move when their chemistry changes.

**What's next step** – Scientists may study how to use resilin’s properties to create new materials for technology or medicine. Meanwhile, this finding encourages more research into how insects survive in extreme environments and why they avoid the ocean.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Lake Malawi insect larvae use strong, stretchy air sacs to dive deep, challenging ideas about insect limits and inspiring new material science research.

articles.title: What The Odyssey reveals about ancient science — from botany to psychiatry
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 23 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02275-0From intelligent ships to clues about eclipses, Homer’s The Odyssey reveals how Bronze Age Greeks understood the world.
articles.content:
Christopher Nolan’s 2026 film The Odyssey puts a twenty-first-century spin on Homer’s epic tale.Credit: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/Shutterstock

In The Odyssey, Homer records the earliest imaginings of autonomous ships guided by what sounds remarkably like artificial intelligence to modern readers. The ships of the Phaeacians, which carry Odysseus home to Ithaca, “know every city, every fertile land”. They “have no steersmen’, and “know by instinct what their crews are thinking and propose to do”.

Homer’s epic tells the adventures and mishaps of Odysseus as he struggles home from the Trojan War. Along with its prequel, The Iliad, it is a foundational piece of literature with roots as far back as 1600 bc. But for all The Odyssey’s fantastical tales of monsters and magic, it also gives glimpses into the science, medicine and technology of the Homeric world.

Here, Nature looks at how researchers are finding the truths behind the legend.

Metallurgy and trade

After being transmitted orally for centuries, The Odyssey was written down during the Iron Age, around 800 bc. Accordingly, it reflects an anachronistic mix of metalwork, from iron knives and gates to bronze spears and swords that reveal its late Bronze Age roots. There are also hints of steel production.

In one passage, Odysseus and his men plunge a spear into the Cyclops’s eye and the hot stake sizzles like when a blade is quenched in water to strengthen it during smithing: a technique that works for steel, but not for pure iron or bronze. Whoever composed that passage, suggests Michael Wright, a craftsman and ex-curator at the Science Museum in London, “witnessed the preparation of a tool with a steel edge”.

Archaeologists have found other details that echo Homer’s text during excavations of the Mycenaean Palace of Nestor near Pylos, Greece. These include vessels made from a mix of bronze, silver and gold, and a rare depiction of a ‘fenestrated’ axe with holes in, dating to around 1450 bc. The holes might explain a puzzling archery challenge that takes place after Odysseus finally returns home, involving shooting an arrow through a line of twelve axes. “The more we excavate, the more we confirm,” says archaeologist Sharon Stocker at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio.

The Odyssey argues for the existence of long-distance trading networks between late Bronze Age civilizations. Archaeologists didn’t find evidence of such trade until the 1980s, when they discovered a fourteenth-century bc shipwreck at Ulu Burun in southern Turkey, packed with luxury treasures from Europe, Africa and Mesopotamia.

Such archaeological discoveries show that people from the eastern Mediterranean were “voyaging all over the Mediterranean much earlier than we would have believed”, says Brendan Foley, a naval and maritime archaeologist at Lund University in Sweden.

The shipwreck was a small, slow cargo ship, around 15 metres long. Odysseus’s ship had 50 oarsmen, implying it was a much longer, narrower ship optimized for speed, says Foley.

Archaeologists found a sanctuary dedicated to the worship of Odysseus that dates back to some time between the fourth and first century bc on the Greek island of Ithaca.Credit: Massimo Pizzocaro/Alamy

Botany and poisons

The Odyssey mentions a range of plant-related drugs, poisons and antidotes. Helen of Troy uses a drug called nepenthe to banish grief, while the sorceress Circe gives Odysseus’s men a potion that makes them forget their homeland and take the form of pigs.

Researchers hunting down nepenthe’s real-life origins say that it could contain plants such as henbane and mandrake, which contain compounds that block the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. These were widely used in the ancient world as painkillers and anaesthetics, says Rafael Molina-Venegas, a botanist at the Doñana Biological Station in Seville, Spain.

In the poem, Hermes gives Odysseus a mysterious herb called moly to protect him from Circe’s potion. It is described as having a black root and a flower like milk. Molina-Venegas and his colleague Rodrigo Verano have suggested that moly could refer to a group of local plants, including sea daffodils (Pancratium spp.), that have white flowers, dark bulbs and inhibit the action of henbane and mandrake.

Colour perception

The nineteenth-century British Prime Minister William Gladstone noted that Homer’s colour palette was extremely limited — mostly variations of white and black, with a few mentions of purple and red. He found Homer’s descriptions of a “purple” rainbow and “wine dark” sea particularly vexing, and suggested that the Greeks’ eyes were less evolved than ours are. An article in Nature in 1886 argued that Homer was often really describing something’s luminosity rather than its colour2.

How AI is unlocking ancient texts — and could rewrite history

Far from not seeing in colour, says Mark Bradley, a classicist at the University of Nottingham, UK, the Greeks had a different way of organizing their visual world3. Today, thanks to Isaac Newton, we understand colour as related to the wavelength of light, but for the Greeks, says Bradley, colours were inseparable from physical objects, and would have included all of their multisensory properties and connotations.
